source.title: The Persian Rug: solving toy models of superposition using large-scale symmetries
source.authors: Aditya Cowsik; Kfir Dolev; Alex Infanger

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equation and text formatting is imperfect, but the relevant content is readable.
record.tranche_reason: It tests the toy superposition claim using the same sparse autoencoder setting but focuses on effective-matrix statistics, analytic bounds, and large-dimension symmetry rather than directly measuring feature-vector angles as in the original work.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on effective-matrix diagonals, biases, off-diagonal interference, and reconstruction loss. It also discusses findings from other papers; those cited findings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Trains the Elhage et al. toy ReLU autoencoder on permutation-symmetric sparse data. It measures effective-matrix (W = Wout·Win) statistics and loss against a linear baseline across p, nd/ns and ns. This bears directly on V1 (interference, regularity, sparsity-dependent benefit), though it uses different measures from the original.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that trained models implement the optimal statistically permutation-symmetric algorithm (loss matches the Persian rug). They further argue that ReLU is near-optimal among elementwise/selection decoders, ruling out SAE activation tweaks beyond constant-factor gains.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the sparse autoencoder toy setting and reconstruction objective associated with the original work, but restricts the analysis to permutation-symmetric data and large input dimension, then studies effective-matrix statistics and constructs optimized Persian rug weights.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported regularity depends on ns: symmetry and Gaussianity of interference improve with increasing ns. At small ns, the off-diagonal uniformity result is reported only for large p. Loss behavior varies with p and nd/ns.

fits_no_version.finding: Analytically, any elementwise or filtering activation replacing ReLU improves reconstruction loss by at most a constant factor; the dominant error is noisy feature magnitudes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-layer affine+ReLU sparse decoders (SAE-like) are near-optimal among elementwise/selection decoders, with loss ~p²/r up to log factors.

record.problems: The empirical trends are often presented as heatmaps without exact values in the text. The paper focuses on permutation-symmetric data and does not directly measure encoded feature-vector angles. The summary gives inconsistent conditions for some loss scalings; detailed sections also state differing regimes.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise qualifying result rows were omitted. Cited results from Elhage et al. and other papers were not included.

untested.parts: Angles or near-orthogonality of individual feature vectors; a discrete phase transition or phase diagram; non-uniform feature importance; correlated features; polytope-style geometry in small models (only permutation-symmetric, mostly large-ns data studied).
All: no neuron-level polysemanticity or importance-based allocation measured (uniform importance only).
All: SAE features in real models not examined.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. Most empirical results are heatmaps without exact values in the text. r7 and r10 are derivations rather than measurements, so they do not ground verdicts on their own.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly measure angles between individual encoded feature vectors or establish their near-orthogonality. Its principal empirical regime is permutation-symmetric data with large input dimension, not a general range of data structures.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition, or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
Does not measure feature representations in LLMs or evaluate SAE recovery in LLMs.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: trained toy model (exemplar; individual checkpoint name not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the effective matrix W = Wout Win and bias components.
rows.measure: Diagonal values, off-diagonal values, and bias values
rows.value: Diagonal components are around 1.29 ± .01 (one standard deviation); off-diagonal components are approximately mean-zero; bias elements are around −.18 ± .01.
rows.uncertainty: One standard deviation, as stated for the diagonal and bias values; not stated for the off-diagonal description.
rows.note: The paper describes the off-diagonal terms as smaller fluctuations around zero, but this measurement does not directly establish angles between encoded feature vectors.
rows.check: Single exemplar (p=4.5%, ns=512; nd not given). Large uniform diagonals and small mean-zero off-diagonals are what V1's near-orthogonal superposed storage predicts, so 'observed' fits better than 'partial'.

rows.subject: toy_network (low-rank effective matrix; analytic result)
rows.operation_detail: Derived a lower bound on off-diagonal interference variance for a low-rank matrix with equal diagonal entries.
rows.measure: Lower bound on mean off-diagonal variance
rows.note: The text states equality holds only for a symmetric, maximum-rank W with all nonzero eigenvalues equal; it proposes a scaled projector as a saturating form.
rows.check: Analytic Welch-type bound under assumed symmetry, not a measurement of trained models, so no observed/absent state applies. It is a theoretical argument relevant to V1's interference limit.

rows.subject: trained toy models (aggregate across plotted models)
rows.operation_detail: Compared reconstruction-loss curves for nonlinear trained models against linear models as compression ratio varies.

conditions.value: representative parameters; exact values not stated

rows.baseline: Linear-model loss curve; exact values not stated
rows.value: The nonlinear model has an immediate loss drop and outperforms the linear model until near nd/ns ≈ 1; at high sparsity, loss falls to zero near nd/ns ≈ 0.
rows.note: The paper says the slope and duration of the initial loss fall depend on p; exact curve values are not given in the text.

rows.subject: Persian rug model
rows.size_stated: Figure 1 uses ns = 256 and nd = 40; other sizes not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared reconstruction loss with trained toy models.

conditions.value: varies in the loss curves; individual values not stated

rows.baseline: Corresponding trained-model loss; exact values not stated
rows.value: The Persian rug model's loss is described as essentially the same as the trained model's; the discussion says the loss matched closely.
rows.note: This engineered comparator is constructed to have the stated large-scale symmetries and an optimized σ.
rows.check: The Persian rug is the authors' own forward-engineered construction, not a trained subject. It is relevant only as evidence that trained models reach the optimal statistically symmetric loss.

source_check.correct: The forward-engineered Persian rug construction closely matches trained-model reconstruction loss. Retain this as a methodological comparison; as a standalone V1 effect row, use cannot_determine rather than observed.
source_check.problem: This is the study's own constructed method compared with trained models; matching loss alone does not establish that trained features exhibit V1.

rows.subject: toy_network (analytic loss analysis)
rows.operation_detail: Derived loss behavior in the high-sparsity regime as a function of p and compression ratio r = nd/ns.
rows.value: The text gives L → p/3 + O(p²) as r → 0; it also derives an upper bound of order (p²/r) log(1/p) in the stated regime r ≪ 1 and pr ≫ 1, and a lower bound of order p²/r up to logarithmic corrections in its stated high-sparsity regime.
rows.note: The paper's summary contains an internally inconsistent condition for the O(p) and O(p²/r) scalings; this row preserves the conditions stated in the detailed derivations rather than resolving that inconsistency.
rows.check: Analytic loss-scaling derivation, not a measurement. The summary's stated regimes are inconsistent ('pr ≪ 1' given for both scalings).

relationships.condition: Trained toy ReLU autoencoders, permutation-symmetric data, large ns
relationships.reason: Diagonals are large and uniform with small mean-zero off-diagonal interference (r1), and off-diagonal statistics concentrate and become Gaussian as ns grows (r4, r5). The nonlinear model beats the linear baseline, with a p-controlled loss drop (r8).
relationships.display_finding: Diagonal weights were large and uniform, with small mean-zero off-diagonal interference whose statistics concentrated and became Gaussian as ns grew. The nonlinear model beat the linear baseline, with a loss drop controlled by p.

relationships.condition: Large-ns permutation-symmetric regime: nature of the 'regular geometry'
relationships.reason: Regularity holds only in large-scale statistics; individual off-diagonal weights look like noise. A differently structured construction matches trained loss, so the microscopic geometry is irrelevant (r1, r5, r9; text Sec. 3.3, 5.1).
relationships.display_finding: Regularity held only in large-scale statistics, and individual off-diagonal weights looked like noise. A differently structured construction matched the trained loss, so the microscopic geometry did not matter.
